slides.title: From "make me something" to a request you can verify
slides.text: When you chat, you leave gaps. The AI can't leave a gap blank: it fills it with the most likely thing it's seen on the internet. And it fills it well, that's the problem. It gives you back something coherent, orderly, and completely unrelated to your case, and because it's well written, it feels like progress. The doubt coming up right now is this. If the AI understands natural language, why do I have to write like…

slides.title: Practice: Write your weak request, exactly as it comes out
slides.text: Before learning anything, put on record where you were about to start. Write in a single line what you would have asked ChatGPT or Claude today about your idea. Do it in your own words and don't clean it up. "Make me a website for my business" works, "I want an assistant to organize my work" works. Don't delete or improve it: you'll need it in task 6 to compare. Save the file as brief.txt on your Desktop. This is…
items: In Windows Notepad, your phone's Notes app, or on paper. Outside the AI.
A brief.txt file on your Desktop with a single sentence in it, yours, written exactly as it came out.

slides.title: The five ingredients of a prompt that works
slides.text: This lesson doesn't ask you to take anything on faith. You're going to send the same request five times, adding one ingredient each time. That way you see with your own eyes what each one buys you. Doing it this way matters because the five aren't equal. Two change the result completely. One changes it a lot less than people online claim. Marta started with eight words: "write me an email to win back customers."…
items: Marta's starting point: "Write me an email to win back customers." What came out: 280 words. They start with "We miss you!", talk about "our passion for what we do," and close with a 10% discount. That text would work just as well for a…

When it answers, copy the whole thing into a notes file on your Desktop called v0.txt. This is your baseline: without it you'll believe you improved instead of seeing it. If your project isn't an email, write the equally vague version of yours. For example: "make me a website for my…

Between 200 and 350 generic words. Look for these four tells: "we miss you," "our passion," a discount you never asked for, and an emoji. Read it thinking of the salon down your street: if it'd work for them too, the experiment is going…

slides.title: Giving examples: the trick that changes the result the most
slides.text: When you write "in a warm tone," the AI has to guess what warm means to you. It's read millions of texts someone called warm: some use casual language, some throw in emojis, some talk about "your everyday life." What it hands you back is the average of all of them, and that average is exactly the text that sounds like nobody in particular. An example of yours kills the guessing outright: it stops interpreting a word…
items: Ask for "a brief, professional follow-up email" and you get back "I hope this message finds you well." Paste below it a real five-line email of yours that starts "Hi Luis, writing about order 4471" and that template-y politeness disappears…

slides.title: Practice: See with your own eyes how much a single example changes
slides.text: Open a new chat (the button is top left and usually says "New chat" or a + sign). Paste only TEST A and send. Copy the answer into a notepad. Now open ANOTHER new chat, don't continue in the same one, because if you do, the AI remembers the previous exchange and the comparison is worthless. In that second chat, paste only TEST B. Put both answers side by side and look at three things: length, whether it's casual or…

slides.title: Saving your prompts and reusing them every day
slides.text: A good prompt almost never comes out on the first try. It comes out on the fourth attempt, after you've told the AI three times: no, not like that, shorter, no exclamation points. That fourth attempt is the one worth money, and it's exactly the one that ends up buried in the middle of a thirty-message conversation you won't even remember having in two weeks. Chat history looks like an archive, but it isn't: it sorts…

slides.title: Practice: Write down what you ask the AI every week
slides.text: Write a list of things you've asked an AI for more than once in the last month. Don't stop to word them nicely: five lines of three words each is fine. Think boring and repeated, not brilliant: answering customer emails, summarizing meetings, writing copy for your website, pulling tasks out of meeting minutes, translating messages. If you get more than eight, cross out until you're down to five: those are what…
items: In a phone note or on paper, no AI open yet

A list of three to five requests, each written as something you do, starting with a verb. If any line is a topic instead of a task (you wrote "marketing" instead of "write the newsletter email"), rewrite it.

slides.title: When the answer doesn't work: correcting course
slides.text: The AI can't see your face. When you read its answer and something bugs you, you know exactly what it is; it has no way of finding out. A correction only works if it carries new information, and the formula that works has three parts: what part is wrong, why it's wrong for your specific case, and what you want instead. Skip the third and the AI guesses again, and guessing is exactly what it already got wrong the…

slides.title: Practice: Provoke a generic answer on purpose
slides.text: Click "New chat" (top left, the paper-and-pencil icon) and paste the request below exactly as it is, without adding anything of your own. This is on purpose: you want to see a generic answer up close so you can spot one in two seconds from now on. When it arrives, read only the first sentence of each paragraph.

Between 200 and 500 words that would work just as well for a hair salon, an accounting firm, or a bike shop. Words that will almost certainly show up: passion, commitment, quality, our team, the customer at the center. Not a single fact…

slides.title: What would prevent your project from being handed off?
slides.text: Use one case you actually observed. Name the evidence, the risk and the next check. There is no automatically correct option for this open question.
items: Missing evidence
Unreliable repeated event
Unknown permission
No recovery owner
